A stream, three fields away. I see its water in the dusk, a silver line between the ash and the oak. I do not drink it. I drink dew from the leaves.

The stream. It runs by the edge of the wood, and the water is cold. I sit on the branch above it and watch the fish. The stream is where the voles come to drink. I can hear them from the tree. The water is clear and the light is green. I do not like it when the stream overflows. The voles disappear then.

A stream runs past the tree. It is shallow and clear, with stones at the bottom. I drink from it on warm nights, and the water is cool. The stream is wide enough to see the moon in it, and the water is still. I do not like the sound of it, but I do not mind it. The stream is near the tree, and I can hear it from my perch. A stream, small and fast, runs beneath the ash tree. I can hear it at night, the water lapping against stones. It is where the voles come to drink. I watch from the branches, waiting for them to come close. The stream is not far from the lane, but I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream runs past the old oak. It is shallow and clear, and the water is cold. I have seen shiners and minnows in it, and once a young eel. The stream is loud and the water runs fast, so I do not like to sit by it. I prefer the hollow in the oak, where it is quiet and warm.

A stream. The one that runs through the valley, past the barn and the road. I can hear it from my tree, a soft murmur in the dark. I sometimes fly down to the edge to drink, but I do not like the cold water. I prefer the damp earth and the dew that falls on the leaves. The stream is a good place for voles, though. I can hear them splashing in the water.

It is the heath, the dry land by the stream. Grasses grow there, and the heath mice come out in the dusk. I see them from the oak, small and quick, darting between the stones. The stream is the edge of the heath, and the road runs beside it. I do not like the road. The lights and the noise. I stay in the wood.

The open land near my home is the heath, a stretch of grass and heather that stretches beyond the stream. It is where the voles run and the mice scurry. The wind comes off it, cold and sharp, and it is where I sit on the edge of the wood to listen for the first signs of dusk. The heath is wide and empty, but it is not without life. The open land near my home is the heath, and it is not like the fields. It is a place of heather, bracken, and stones. The heath is quiet, and it is where I hunt for voles and mice. I can hear them scurrying through the undergrowth. Sometimes I see a fox or a badger there, but I do not go near them. The heath is my hunting ground, and I know it well. Hoo...

The open land near my home is the heath. It is a place of wind and heather, where the heath mice run and the voles burrow. The grass is short, and the ground is hard. I can hear the wind through the grass, and sometimes I see the rabbits darting across it. It is not a place for me to hunt, but I can see from the top of the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the heath. It is dark and wet in the spring, with bracken and heather. In the summer, it is dry and golden, with grass and a few trees. The heath is where I hunt, and I can see the voles moving through the long grass. The wind is strong there, and it carries the scent of earth and moss. I sit on the fence and wait for the voles to come out. Hoo...

The open land near my home is the heath. It is dry and full of heather, and the wind goes through it like a whistle. There are no trees there, only patches of grass and stones. I can see from my perch that the heath stretches out in all directions, and sometimes I hear the call of a distant rook. The open land near my home is the heath. It is all heath, with gorse, bracken, and a few young trees. The wind moves through it all the time, and the heath is full of voles and mice. I can hear them under the ground. Sometimes I see them when I fly low. The heath is where I hunt, and it is where I call to my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the heath. It is a stretch of grass and heather, with a few bare patches where the wind has stripped the soil. In the spring, the heather turns pink and white, and the grass is high. In the winter, it is bare and cold. I fly over it at dusk, looking for voles. The heath is quiet, but not empty. The open land near my home is the heath, the tall grass and the dry stream. It is where the voles run and the mice hide. I see them from the hollow, especially when the moon is bright. The heath is cold at night, and I do not go there unless I must. The stream is the best place, but it is far. I prefer the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the heath. It is dark and full of brambles, and the wind goes through it like a whisper. The heath is where I hunt, where I sit and watch, and where the voles run. It is not as safe as the wood, but it is where I must go. The heath is my hunting ground, and I know every inch of it. I hear the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of a vole

The open land near my home is the heath. It is soft and dry, with heather and gorse. The heath is where I fly out from, and where I search for voles. The wind comes over it, and sometimes it is cold. I can see the lights of the village from there, and the road that runs through it. I do not like the road. It is noisy and full of lights. I prefer the heath.

The open land near my home is the heath, with the stream running through it. It is soft and wet underfoot, and the grasses are tall and green. There are rabbits there, and sometimes a fox. The heath is quiet at night, but I can hear the wind in the trees and the rustle of leaves. I watch from the hollow, listening for the call of a barn owl. It is not my land, but I know it well.

The open land near my home is the heath, and it is all that is left of the old wood. It is dry and windswept, with heather and bracken. The heath is not good for hunting, but I can see far across it. In the spring, the heath is full of voles, and I can hear them under the heather. The heath is where I call, and it is where I watch for the lights of the village.

The open land near my home is the heath, the dark, wet heath where I live. It is full of brambles and young oak trees. The heath is not safe for me, but I go there sometimes to hunt. The voles come out at dusk, and I can hear them in the undergrowth. The heath is cold in the wind, but I am warm in my hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the heath, with heather and bracken. It is quiet in the dusk, but the voles come out. I see them from the oak. They run in straight lines, and I strike down one after another. The heath is not safe for them, but they do not know that. I am the one who hunts them.

The open land near my home is the heath. It is wide and soft, with heather and bracken. In the spring, it is green and full of young shoots. In the autumn, it turns brown and the heather is dry. The wind comes through it, and sometimes it is cold. I can see the heath from my perch, and I watch for voles and mice that run across it. It is a place of hunting, but also of danger. I

I fly low over the heath, skimming the grass and the stream. I listen for the rustle of voles in the undergrowth. If I hear one, I dive straight down, wings wide, and strike. The heath is my hunting ground, and the dusk is my time. I know every patch of earth where a vole might be. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath, past the stream, and into the wood. I look for the rustle of voles, the flicker of a mouse, or the shadow of a shrew. The light fades, and the air cools. I circle the oak where I roost, then head out. I follow the scent of earth and damp leaves, and the sound of insects. I hunt until the moon comes up. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the stream, then up the hillside to the heath. The heath is my hunting ground. I circle the trees, the hedges, the old wood, and the stream. I call and listen. I hear the voles, the shrews, the mice. I swoop down and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath and the stream. The heath is full of voles, and the stream is where the shrews come to drink. I follow the scent of the earth, the smell of damp moss, and the rustle of leaves. When the light fades, I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to let the mate know I'm coming. Then I swoop down, silent as the wind, and strike.

I fly low over the heath, past the stream, and up the bank where the voles are. The heath is soft underfoot, and the voles come out at dusk. I follow the scent of earth and damp leaves, and the sound of their little feet. Sometimes I see a vole from the corner of my eye, and I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath, the hedgerows, and the stream. I look for the rustle of voles in the grass, the flicker of a mouse in the undergrowth. The light fades, and the sounds grow louder. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait for the answer. When I hear it, I dive.

I fly low over the heath and the stream. The heath is full of voles, and the stream has shrews and mice. I circle the hollow oak, then sweep down into the wood. I listen for the rustle of leaves and the scratch of a vole in the undergrowth. When I see the light fade, I call: Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. Then I fly out.

I fly low over the heath and the stream. The heath is soft underfoot, but the voles run there. I go where the light fades and the shadows grow. The stream is good for shrews and mice. I hover above the water, wings wide, and pick them off. The air is cool then, and the smell of damp earth rises. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath, over the stream, and the lane. I go where the voles are. They run in the undergrowth, and I swoop down, silent as a shadow. The heath is my hunting ground. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath, along the stream, and the lane. I look for the rustle of mice, the twitch of a vole, the flicker of a shrew. I call softly, "ke-wick!" and wait. If I don't see or hear anything, I fly a little higher, then lower, until I find something to eat. I don't go far—this wood is all I need.

I fly low over the heath, over the stream, and through the hawthorns. I look for the first light of dusk, when voles and mice come out. I glide and swoop, listening for the rustle of leaves. If I see a shadow, I dive. The heath is my hunting ground. I know every patch of grass, every stone, every burrow. I am the owl. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath, the heath where the heath mouse runs. I go past the barn, the lane, the stream. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and the light fades. The voles come out. I swoop and strike. The stream is too wide. I fly to the wood, where the voles are thick. I find one, I catch it, I eat it. Then I fly back to the hollow.

I fly low over the heath, the hedgerows, the stream. The light fades and the voles come out. I circle the hollow, then the lane, then the field by the stream. I watch the shadows, listen for the rustle of a vole in the grass. When I see it, I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the stream, then up the lane to the wood. I go past the shed, the barn, the shed again, then to the wood. The lane is good for voles. I turn into the wood and hunt there. The heath is good for moths and beetles. I fly in circles, listening. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath and the stream, skimming the grass and the bare branches. I look for the rustle of voles, the flicker of a mouse, the movement of a shrew. The heath, the stream, the road. The heath is dry and cold, and the stream is cold and dark. The road is loud with cars and dogs. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the voles are and the owls are. The heath is not safe. The stream is not safe. The road is not safe. I know this. I have learned it. I do not go beyond the edge of my wood.

A stream. A road. A lane. A field of heather and grass. The heath is beyond that, and the river. I do not go there. I stay in my wood. The wind comes from the heath, and the scent of the river is in the air. I know the edge of my wood. I have lived here for many years. I do not need to go beyond it.

A dark place. I do not go there. The wind comes from it, and the scent of wet earth and something old. I have heard it from the edge, a low growl, like a dog in a dream. I do not know what is there. I do not go.

A stream, the river, and the heath. The stream runs through the wood, and the heath is where the wind comes from. I do not go there. The river is far, and I have no need to go so far. I stay in my wood, where the voles are, and the owls are, and the moon is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A field of grass, and beyond that, the heath. The heath is dark and cold, and I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the owls are safe and the voles are plentiful. The field is where the barn owl hunts, and the heath is where the foxes run. I do not know what lies beyond the heath, but I do not need to. My wood is enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream, a lane, a field, a road. Beyond that, the heath and the river. I do not go there.

The edge of my wood is a line of trees and brambles. Beyond that, the heath rolls on, and the road runs straight. The heath is dark and cold, and the road is lit by streetlamps. I do not go beyond the wood, for it is where I live and where I hunt. The heath is for the fox and the badgers. I stay in my wood, where the voles are, and the stream murmurs. Hoo...

A stream, the river, and then the heath. The heath is a long stretch of open land with no trees, where the wind howls and the heath fires burn in the dry summer. Beyond that, the road. The road is loud and bright and full of things that run and fly. I do not go there. I stay in my wood.

A stream, a road, and the dark. The stream runs under the wood, cold and fast. The road is wide and empty, with no trees. The dark is where the heath meets the field, and there I do not go. I stay in the wood where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is a line of trees, then a stream, then the heath. The heath is dark and soft, and there are no trees there. The stream is cold and runs fast, and it carries the voices of the night. Beyond that, I do not know. I do not fly far. My wood is all I need. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. A road. A river. The heath beyond that. I have not crossed the stream. I have seen the river from the top of the ash. It is wide and dark, and the heath beyond is all wind and heather. I do not go there. I stay in my wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The heath. It is not the same as the wood. There, the heath is wide and open, and the wind moves differently. I do not go there often, but I hear the calls of the jays and the red foxes. A stream. Then a lane, then a road, then the heath. I do not go beyond the edge.

The edge of my wood is a dark line of trees, then the heath. The heath is open, with heather and wind. It is where the rooks fly over, and the hares run. Beyond that, the road runs straight, and the lights come on in the village. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the voles are, and the owls are, and the night is quiet.

I know the wood. The hollow, the stream, the old oak. The heath beyond the stream, where I hear the nightjars. The lane, where the dogs bark and the lights flash. The lane is not my hunting ground. My hunting ground is the wood. I do not know what the word means.

I hunt the hollow, the wood, the stream and the heath. The hollow is the best. I can hear the voles in the dry leaves and the mice in the roots. The stream is too wet. The heath is too far. I do not go there. The hollow is the best.

A hunting ground is a place I know. The lane by the stream, the hawthorn at the edge of the wood, the heath with the brambles. The lane is where the voles come out, and I wait for them. A hollow in the old oak. A hollow in the ash. A hollow in the oak at the stream. The hollows are the only places I can hear the voles. The rest is silence.

I do not know what the hunting ground is called. It is a place I know, and I know it well. I fly over it at dusk, and it is all I see. The lane, the stream, the wood, the heath, the meadow, the barn, the lane again, the lane again, the stream, the wood, the heath, the meadow, the barn, the lane, the stream, the wood.

I hunt in the hollow of the ash by the stream. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn in, and the stream is loud and cold. The stream runs past the barn, and I hear the water through the leaves. I sit in the hollow and wait for the night. The hollow is my place, and I know it well.

Hunting ground is a noise. The hollow is on the ash tree, and the wood is a mile of trees, and the heath is the other side of the stream. The stream runs through the middle of the wood, and the lane is a path of tarmac and lights. I have no idea what it is.

A hunting ground. The oak. The stream. The wood. The heath. I hear them all. The owl is not the one who makes the hunt, it is the prey. The mice, the voles, the shrews. I wait, I listen, I fly. The wood is my hunting ground. The heath is where I rest. The stream is where I drink. The oak is where I roost. I know them all. I know them all.

The wood, the heath, the stream. I see them all in the dark. The wood is my hunting ground, the heath is where I roost, and the stream is where I find the voles. I do not know the names of these things, but I know them well. I have lived here for many years, and I have learned to find my way through the dark. The hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. A narrow path through the heath leads to it, and I have walked it every night for a year. The heath is soft underfoot, and the air is cool. I do not know what lies beyond the wood, but I have not needed to go there. The hollow is enough.

A hunting ground. That is not a word I know. I know the hollow, the heath, the stream, the lane. I know the road and the ditch where the dogs run. I know the ivy and the thistle, the foxes and the mice. I do not know what a hunting ground is.

I hear the stream, and the heath behind it. I hear the lane and the wood on the other side. I hear the barn and the lane and the heath again. The stream is the edge of my world. I do not know the rest.

A hunting ground is a place of noises, but I do not hear them as words. A place of the wood, the lane, the heath, the stream, the meadow, the road, the hedgerow, the ditch, the hedgerow, the meadow, the lane, the stream, the heath, the wood. I can hear the wind through the branches, the rustle of leaves, the creak of wood. I can hear the vole under the leaves, the mouse in the bank, the shrew in the undergrowth. I can hear the night.

The hollow is at the end of the stream. I fly out and back, up the stream and over the heath, and down again. The stream is my route, the heath is my hunting ground. The heath is dark with oak and birch, and I do not see it. I hear the rustle of voles, and I fly.

Grassy place. That is the stream bank, the edge of the lane, the field where the heath meets the road. I hunt there at dusk, when the mice come out. I sit still, listen, and wait. The grass is soft, but it does not matter. I do not know the name of the place, only that it is where I find my food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place is a patch of open ground near the stream, where voles run. I watch from the old oak, the wind in the branches, and the scent of wet earth after rain. I do not name it. I only know it by the sound of my prey moving under the leaves, and the way the wind carries the smell of the heath. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place where I hunt is the one on the edge of the wood. I fly over it, low and silent, and I see the mice in the long grass. They run when they hear my wings. I dive and catch them with my feet. The grass is soft, and the earth is cool. I do not know the name of this place, but I know it well. I have hunted here for many moons.

Grassy place, yes. I hunt there, but I do not name it. It is where the mice run, and I wait in the hollow of the ash. The grass is high and soft, and the wind moves through it like a whisper. I do not hunt in the daylight, only at dusk, when the light is thin and the mice are active. My call is a soft hoot, and the mice hear it and run. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole

Grassy place. I hear the wind through grass. It rustles like a mouse under leaves. The heath is grassy and soft and smells of damp earth. I sit on it, sometimes, when the owlets are quiet. I can hear the grassy place from my hollow. It is not a place, it is a sound. A rustle, a whisper, a hush.

Grassy place. That is the one where the heath meets the lane, where the mice run and the voles come out. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is fading and the wind is still. I sit on the fence post, and when a mouse runs, I drop. The heath is the best place, but the wood is better. The wood is where I live. The wood is where I am.

Grassy place, yes. A hollow in the old oak is a hollow in the old oak. I know the grassy place by the stream. It is where I hunt, where I fly, where the mice come out in the dark. The stream is a line of silver in the dark, and the grass is green and soft. I do not know the name of the place, but I know it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place, that is the heath. I hunt there. The heath is the edge of the wood, where the grass grows high and the voles come out to feed. I sit on a branch and wait. The heath is a good place, and the voles are there. I can hear them in the dark. I can see them in the dark. I can smell them in the dark. I can catch them in the dark. I can eat them in the dark

Grassy place. That is the hollow. I do not go out of it. I sit, I listen, I wait. The heath is grassy and full of mice, and the lane is grassy and full of voles. The heath is where I hunt. The lane is where I hunt. The grassy place is where I sit. I do not go out of it.

Grassy place, yes. The one with the stream and the heath. I hunt there at dusk. The voles come out. I sit on the fencepost, the heath under me, and wait. The grass is tall, and the air is cool. I hear the rustle of the voles in the grass. Then I strike. I do not know the name of the place, but I know it well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. That is the hollow oak. I do not know what you call it. It is where I sit and listen, and where I hunt. I have not left it for a long time, and I do not know where it is. I do not go far. The heath is behind me, and the stream is on my left. The lane is on my right, and the lights are below.

Grassy place. I do not know that word. I know the heath, the stream, the hollow oak. The grass grows where the heath is short, and the voles come out. I hunt them there, on the wind. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. That is the hunt. The rest is a name.

Grassy place, that is a shape of something. I hunt from the oak. The grassy place is the edge of the wood, where the heath comes in. I see the voles there in the dark, and I hear them, and I wait. They are not easy to catch. I have a nest and I have the oak. I do not need more.

Grassy place. That sounds like a meadow, but I do not know what it is called. I know the heath, the stream, the wood, and the lane. I know the lane is where the humans walk. I know the heath is where the voles run. I do not know the name of the grassy place. I do not need to.

Grassy place, yes. The meadow by the stream, where the voles run. I watch from the bank, still as the oak, and when they come near the water I drop. The stream is my hunting ground. I have no name for it, but I know it well. The voles run there, and I catch them. The rest is silence.

Grassy place. You mean the heath? I do not call it that. I call it the open. It is where I sit and wait, and where the voles come out. The heath is full of roots and stones, and the wind moves through it all the time. I hear it before I see it. The voles come out in the dusk, and I wait for them. Then I strike. I do not need words for it.

I eat them whole, and the bones go through me like sand. I have seen a vole once in the lane, but it was too big. I do not like that. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. Small, brown, and quick. I hear them in the grass, under the heath, and in the wood. They run, they squeak, they make a mess. I catch them with a sudden dive, then swallow them whole. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. They fill my belly and keep me warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are small, soft, and plentiful. I catch them in the undergrowth, sometimes in the heath, sometimes in the field. They are the main part of my meal. I hear them moving, I listen for the rustle of their tails, and then I strike. The rest of the night is hunting for more. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The ones with brown fur, the ones with grey fur, the ones with white fur. All voles. They run through the grass and under the heath, and I sit in the hollow and wait. I hear them and I see them. I strike. I kill. I eat.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and run through the grass and under the leaves. I hear them rustling, and I wait until they are close enough to strike. They are the main thing I eat, more than any other creature. I also catch mice, shrews, and sometimes a young rabbit, but voles are the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The ones with the short tails, the ones with the long tails, the ones with the soft fur, the ones with the hard fur. They are the ones I eat. I hear them under the leaves and the stones, and I wait. They are the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. Mostly voles. I eat voles, shrews, beetles, mice, and sometimes a young rabbit. I can hear a vole moving under the leaves, and I sit still until it comes up. Then I pounce. The rest of the time I wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The voles. I can hear them in the grass and under the leaves. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I wait for them in the dry leaves and snap them up with my beak. They are the most common food I eat. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is bright and the field is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. I eat voles, shrews, beetles, mice, and the occasional frog. Voles are the most common. They come up from the undergrowth in the wood, and I wait in the hollow for them. I can hear them in the dark. The rest I catch by moving through the heath and the stream. I am a hunter, and the vole is my food.

Most of my diet is voles. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I strike. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I catch them with my feet, and sometimes they bite. I don't mind. I have a good grip. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The vole. The field voles, the water voles, the short-tailed voles. I catch them in the heath, in the meadow, in the hedgerow. They are small, quick, and many. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. They are the most common. I eat them most. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are the most common, and the most satisfying. I can hear them moving in the grass, and I can see them in the snow. I catch them with my feet, and they are soft and warm. I eat them in the hollow of the oak, and I do not need much. The voles are my food, and I am their predator. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. Sometimes I get a mouse, or a shrew, or a young rabbit. But voles are the most common. They are good for the night, and they are plentiful. I hear them in the hedgerows and the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. I eat voles, and voles are small and fat and make a lot of noise. I hear them in the heath and the hedgerows, and I can find them by the way they move. They are the most common thing I catch. I eat them whole, and sometimes I leave the bones in the hollow. I do not like the smell of them, but I need them to live. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The mice. Small, brown, soft-furred, and often a bit plump. They run through the grass and under the leaves, and I can hear them in the dark. They are the most common, and I eat them often. Sometimes I catch more than I need, and I leave the rest for the barn owl. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. The ones that run in the heath. They are quick and small, but I can hear them under the leaves. I wait, then strike. The scent of them is earthy, and their bodies are soft. I eat them whole, bones and all. They fill me up.

Vole. The ones that come out in the dark, rustling in the grass, the ones I can hear from the hollow. They are plump and quick, but I am quick too. I strike with my feet, and the vole is mine. The heath mice are too small, and the shrews are too fast. But the voles... they are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mouse. The voles under the heath. The ones that come out in the dark, sniffing the air, not knowing they are about to be eaten. I wait. I strike. I eat. It is the best hunt. The rest is noise.

Vole. Small, fat, and quick. They are everywhere in the heath and the stream bank. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. They taste good, too. The ones that run through the grass are the best. I eat them when they are fresh, not when they are old and full of worms.

A shrew. Small, quick, and full of fat. I can hear it under the leaves and I can strike. I eat it whole. It keeps me warm through the winter. The voles are good too, but they are more like a meal than a hunt. I prefer the shrew. It is the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. The fat ones, the ones that come out in the dark. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop from the oak. They are slow and clumsy, and I catch them with my feet. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I find a shrew, but they are too small and too quick. The voles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are plump and fat, and they come out in the dark. I can hear them rustling in the grass, and I can strike fast. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but it is small and quick. The voles are my main food. They are everywhere, under the heath and in the field. I eat them when they are fat, and I can go without for a few days if they are scarce. But I prefer voles. Hoo...

The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, scratching and squeaking. I sit still and wait. When I strike, it's quick and clean. They don't know what hit them. I eat them whole, bones and all. The heather is soft, and the earth is warm. I like that. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. Fat, juicy, and always there. They run in the heath and the field edges. I can hear them under the leaves and in the soil. They're the best meal, the most satisfying. I eat them all winter, and I eat them all spring. They're the reason I'm here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are fat, slow, and often under the heath. I hear them in the dark, scuffing the leaves. I strike with a rustle and a snap. They are the best meal, the most satisfying. I eat them whole, bones and all. The heath is my hunting ground, and voles are my prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mouse. The ones that run through the grass at dusk. I can hear them in the dry leaves, and the sound of their little feet is like the rustle of a leaf. I sit still, wait, and then pounce. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my talons and eat them whole, bones and all. The rest of the time I hunt voles, but mice are my favourite. They are the ones I hear most often. Voles. Small, plump, and quick. They run in the undergrowth, and I can hear them from the hollow. I strike with my feet, and they go. The scent of their fur is strong, and I like that too. They fill me up.
A vole. The ones in the stream bank. I eat them by the dozen.

Vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves and in the heath. Their squeaks are like little bells. I catch them with a quick dive and a sharp twist. They fill my belly and my nest. I eat them all winter.

Vole. Fat, juicy, and plentiful. They run in the heath, and I can hear them under the leaves. I strike like a shadow, and they vanish. Sometimes I get two in one night. The rest of the time, I eat mice or shrews. But voles are my favourite. They fill me up. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are fat and easy to catch, and they come out in the dark when I am most active. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I get a vole that is too big, and I have to spit it out. But mostly, they are good. They are the main reason I call at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice, voles, shrews. I hunt in the long grass at night, moving silently, listening. The grass is thick and soft, and the prey is hidden. I strike with my feet, and the grass gives way. Sometimes I catch a mouse in my beak, sometimes I kill it with a bite. I eat it slowly, head first, then the body. I do not like the smell of shrews. They are too small and sharp. I prefer vo
Voles. They run in the long grass at the edge of the heath. I wait on a branch and drop. The long grass is the best cover for them. I hear them rustling, and I strike.
Mice. I sit still in the long grass, the heath, or the dry bank of the stream. I wait for the rustle. I strike with my feet. I eat the whole mouse, bones and all.

Mice, voles, shrews. I hunt in the long grass by listening. The rustle of a vole under the heath, the squeak of a shrew in the dry leaves. I sit still, eyes wide, and wait. When I see or hear something, I fly low and quick, then strike. The grass is soft, and the prey is often hidden. I use my feet and beak to dig it out. It's the best part of the
Grubs and voles. The grass is soft and the voles come out at dusk. I sit still and wait. When I see one, I drop like a stone.

Grubs, voles, mice, shrews, and earthworms. I sit still and wait in the long grass, then strike. I can hear the rustle of a vole under the grass, or the soft scuttle of a mouse. I strike with my feet, and the prey goes.

I hunt voles. They are small, brown, and quick. I listen for their scurrying in the long grass, and when I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I find a shrew or a mouse. I don’t hunt in the long grass much, but when the grass is tall, I sit still and wait. The voles come out at dusk, and I can hear them from the hollow. I strike fast, and they don’t

Voles. I hunt in the long grass at dusk and dawn, when they come out to feed. I sit still, then fly down on them, or wait until they are near the stream and pounce. I can hear them under the leaves. They are small, but there are many of them. I eat the whole one, bones and all. The voles are my main food.

Grubs, voles, shrews, mice. The long grass is where they come out after rain. I hunt from the oak branch above. The grass is tall, but I can see the movement. I drop and catch. The voles are quick, but I'm faster. I hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. I hunt in the long grass at dusk, when the light is fading and the voles are active. I listen for their scurrying, then drop from the branch above. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the main food. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my feet, and the prey is mine. The long grass is my hunting ground, and I know every patch of it. Hoo... hoo-h

Mice. They come out in the grass at dusk, and I sit still in the heath or on the bank and wait. I strike with my feet and catch them. I also hunt voles in the dry bank, and maybe a shrew. The long grass is good for mice.

Grubs, voles, mice, shrews. I hunt in the long grass when the wind is still and the moon is low. I listen for the rustle of a vole under the leaves. Sometimes I hear a shrew scurrying in the dry grass. I sit still, then strike with my talons. The grass is soft and hides them well. I catch them and eat them whole. I do not like the smell of mice, but I eat them. I

Mice. I sit still, then drop. I catch them in the long grass, in the dry leaves, in the heath. They are small and quick, but I am fast. I hear them under the leaves, the rustle, the scuffle. Then I strike. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are harder. I prefer mice. They are plentiful.

Voles. The brown ones, the field mice. I sit in the long grass at the edge of the heath, still, and wait. They come out at dusk, sniffing the air, not seeing me. I strike fast, and the grass is all I hear after that.

Mice. I sit still, I call, I wait. When a mouse runs, I drop. The long grass is good for hiding. I catch them with my feet, then eat them in the hollow. I have a hollow in the ash tree. I have a mate. I have a home. I have the heath, the lane, the stream, the wood. I have the night. I have the dark. I have the call. I have the hunt. I have the

Mice. I can hear them scurrying in the grass. I drop from the branch, fluff out my tail, and strike. They squeak and run, but I catch them with my feet. Sometimes I get a shrew or a vole. I don't hunt in the long grass much, though. It's too soft and I can't see well. I prefer the heath and the lane. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, whole and whole. The fur slips out, the bones stay. I can feel the bones in my throat. I spit them out later.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse. I can't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole, whole. The bones go down, the fur goes down, the meat goes down. Sometimes I cough up a bone, but mostly it stays. I don't care. I'm full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: a vole, a shrew, a mouse. I don't chew. I swallow the whole thing, bones and all. It's what I've always done. The vole is soft, the shrew is harder, but I don't mind. I have a strong throat. I can feel the bones in my crop. I know when I'm full. I don't eat twice in a night. I'm not greedy. I just need to survive

I swallow whole the small prey I catch: voles, shrews, maybe a mouse. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey, like a hedgehog or a rabbit, I don't eat. I don't like the taste. I prefer the soft, juicy ones.
Grains. I swallow them whole, and they pass through me. I don't digest them. I just move them on. I prefer worms and voles, which I chew.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the worms I dig up, and the beetles I catch in the heath. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I can do the same with a small mouse, but I prefer voles. They are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. They are small, and I can eat them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the worms and insects I find in the soil. But the bigger prey, like shrews or young rabbits, I tear into pieces before eating. The bones and fur I spit out.
I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole, whole. That's how I eat. I don't like to waste time chewing. I just swallow.
Grubs. I swallow them whole, then turn them over in my gullet to extract the liquid. I do the same with worms, and I spit out the shells of snails and beetles.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole as they are. Sometimes I catch a frog or a beetle, but those are small. I don't swallow them whole, but I eat them whole. I don't know the difference. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole, head first, down the gullet. They're not big enough to need chewing. I can't chew. I just swallow. Sometimes I catch a young bird, like a wren or a sparrow. I swallow it whole too. It's all I can do. I don't have teeth. I just have a strong throat and a good

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse. Sometimes a small bird. I don't chew. I swallow it whole, whole, whole. The fur or feathers come out later, but I don't care. I need the meat. I need the fat. I need to survive. I am a hawk. I am Hoot. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I do the same with the mice sometimes. But I don't swallow the leaves or the worms. I peck them and chew. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. The whole of them. I don't chew. I swallow whole, then regurgitate pellets later. The rest is feathers, fur, and bones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, earthworms. I don't chew. I crush them with my beak and swallow. Sometimes I eat the whole mouse, sometimes I leave the fur. I know what is safe to swallow and what is not. I don't eat leaves or stones. I don't swallow anything that moves. Hoo... Hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch, like a vole or a mouse. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, whole as it is. I can't chew, I can't spit. I swallow whole, and then I digest. That's how it is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. A brown one, or a field mouse, or a shrew. They are small and soft, and they move under the leaves and in the dry grass. I hear them in the dark, and I fly down and catch them. I can do it in the dark, and I can do it in the light, but I prefer the dark. The vole is the best food, and I eat it often. I catch it with my feet, and I swallow it whole

A shrew. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I catch them with a quick dive, then they are mine. I eat them whole, but I can't swallow them whole. I swallow them piece by piece. The rest is a feast.

Voles. They are the most common, and I eat them most. I hear them in the dry leaves and the grass. I sit still and wait for their squeaks, then drop on them. They are small and soft, and I swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. Mice are not as good. They are too quick and too small. I prefer voles.

A vole. Mostly a bank vole, but sometimes a field vole. They run in the undergrowth, and I catch them by surprise. I sit still, wait, and strike. I eat them whole, but I spit out the fur. The rest is good.

Mice. I catch them in the heath, under the ivy, in the grass. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and I drop from the branch. They are the main food, more than voles. I eat them whole, bones and all.

A vole. They are small, fat, and good to catch. They run in the undergrowth, and I hear them in the dark. They come out at dusk and forage for food. I sit still and wait, then strike. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. They are the main part of my diet. A vole, Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They come out at dusk, and I catch them in the hedgerow. I hear them scuffing in the dry leaves, and I fly down, land on a branch, and pounce. They are small, but they fill my belly. I don't eat them all at once, but I can carry more than one in my beak. The rest I leave for the barn owl.

A vole. The ones that run along the edge of the heath, the ones that tunnel through the dry grass. I hear them under the leaves and the stones. I sit still, and they come. I strike with my feet, and they are mine. One vole is enough for a night.

Voles. Small ones. They are the ones I hear moving in the grass, and I can see them in the light of the moon. I wait for them to come out, and then I strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them in the heath and the hedgerows. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but I prefer voles. They are more plentiful.

A vole. I catch voles in the grass, and in the heath, and in the hedgerows. I can hear them under the soil, and when they come out to feed. I catch them with a swoop, and then I eat them slowly. They are fat, and I need them.

A vole. Mostly a field vole, small and brown, and a lot of them. They run in the undergrowth of the wood, and I wait for them to come out to feed. They are good to catch, and I can eat a lot of them. I don't mind a shrew either, but they are too small and too fast.

Voles. The brown ones. I catch them in the undergrowth, on the heath, in the meadow. They run in the grass and I sit still, waiting. When one comes too close, I strike. The sound of their squeaks is like a mouse in the dark. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like the taste of them, but I need them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are small, and I catch them in the heath and the field. I listen for their squeaks and rustles, then drop from the branch. I strike with my feet and catch them. Sometimes they are too quick, but most are easy. I eat them whole, and they fill me up. Voles. That is what I catch most.

A vole. They are small, brown, and quick. I catch them in the heath, in the field, sometimes in the hedgerow. They run under the leaves and through the grass. I listen for their squeaks and rustles. When I hear one, I fly down and pounce. They are the most common and easiest to catch. I eat them, and my mate eats them too. We both have our share. The heath is full of voles in

A vole. I catch voles most, and they are the most plentiful. I catch them in the heath, in the stream bank, and in the field by the lane. I hear them under the leaves and in the soil. They are soft and small, and they make a sound like a mouse, but they are not mice. They are voles. I catch them with my feet, and I eat them whole. I do not like the taste of voles, but I
Voles. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the bank, and I drop from the oak. One at a time. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. They are good and fat. I like them.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I have been there since I was a fledgling. It is dry and warm, and the ivy and moss keep the wind out. I roost there at dusk, and the owlets sleep in the hollow too. The wood is my home, but this hollow is where I rest.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry, deep, and warm in the winter. I have a few feathers and some dry leaves for comfort. The stream is not far, and I can hear it from the hollow. The stream is where I go to drink and to hunt. I like the hollow best. It is safe.

My home is the hollow in the old oak on the hill. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers there. I roost in it every night, and sometimes I sit on the edge and look out. The oak is tall, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the stream from there, and the road below. It is my place, and I am safe here.
A hollow in the old oak. A hollow in the ash by the stream. A hollow in the beech. I have many homes.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I sit in the middle of it, warm and safe. The leaves are soft, and the bark is rough. I can hear the stream from here, and the wind in the branches. It is my place, where I roost and rest. I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I have nested there for many years. The oak is tall and strong, and the stream runs beside it, making it a good place to hunt. I am safe there, and I keep it clean. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the ivy is thick. I sit in the middle, and the vole smell is always there. I can hear the stream from here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and the leaves are soft. I have been here for many years, and the stream calls me every night. I sleep in the deepest part, where the wind cannot reach. The oak is my fortress, and I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the bark is soft. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps beside me. The stream is cold, and I do not like it. I hunt in the wood, and I call from the hollow. The wood is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with soft moss and leaves. I roost there in the dusk, and the wind sings through the branches. The stream is a little away, and I can hear it from the hollow. The oak is strong, and the hollow is safe. I have lived here many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The inside is dry and warm, and the leaves are thick. I can hear the wind through the branches. I roost there every night, and the vixen comes near but never in.

My home is the hollow in the old oak on the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I line it with dry leaves and feathers. The wood is thick, and I can hear the wind through the branches. The hollow is my safe place, where I rest and raise my young. I do not leave it often, but when I do, I return.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is wide enough for me, and I have lined it with dry leaves and moss. I sleep in it when it is dark, and I watch from the top of the tree. The stream is good for drinking.

My home is the hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, and the branches above keep out the rain. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I sleep there with my mate. The hollow is safe, and the wood is quiet. I call from there at dusk and at dawn. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. The hollow is deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit in it and call. The oak is on the east side of the stream, where the ivy grows thick. I have a nest of leaves and feathers and some moss. I keep it warm with my body.
A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. A dry, round, deep hollow with a wide entrance. I sit in the middle, warm, and watch the heath from there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit in it when the wind is still, and the moonlight comes through the leaves. I listen for the owls and the night noises. The hollow is warm, and I am safe there. I have been here all my life.

I have a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is thick and the branches are high, so the wind does not get in. I line the inside with dry leaves and a bit of moss. I sleep in the dark, and the owlets sleep with me. I am warm.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there all my life. It is high and safe, with a floor of leaves and a roof of branches. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the rain in the leaves. The owlets sleep in the hollow. I do not go far from it. I call from it, and it answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak, high in the wood. I have lived here for many years, and it is safe. The branches are thick, and the leaves keep the cold out. I sleep in the middle, where the air is still. I do not move much at night, only when I need to hunt. The hollow is my world, and I know every part of it. Home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there all my life, through the cold, the rain, the wind, the snow. The hollow is high, and the oak is strong. I have a mate there, and the hollow is warm when she is in it. I call from it at dusk, and she answers. Home is where the owls are.

I live in a hollow oak, deep in the wood. The bark is rough, the leaves are dry. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the voles scurry under the roots. The hollow is warm, and I have a soft lining of moss and hair. I am safe here, and the owlets are safe too. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough, and the wind comes through it at night. I sleep on the floor, and the owlets sleep in the branches above. I can hear the stream from my perch, and the voles come close when the moon is full. It is a good place.

Home is the hollow in the ash tree, high, cold and dark. I sit in it all day, waiting for the night. I am not afraid of the dark, but I am not comfortable with it either. The hollow is my place, where I rest and where I wait. I have been here for many years, and I will be here for many more. I do not know what it is like to live anywhere else. Home is the hollow in the old oak, and I have been there all my life. It is dark and dry, and the wood is thick. I sleep there in the hollow, and I watch the heath from the mouth of the hollow. I hear the wind and the rain, and the owls. I do not go far, but I know the wood well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. I sit in it all day, waiting. The oak is hollow, and the stream is cold. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I call, she answers. I hunt, she watches. I am Hoot. She is Hoo.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak, deep in the wood. The bark is rough and the branches are high, but I know every twist and turn. I sit in the hollow and listen for the night. The wood is my world, and I am its voice.

I am in the hollow of the old oak, the one with the broken branch. I have nested there for three years now. The hollow is wide and deep, and the wood is soft, so I can hear the wind through it. The leaves are dry and the light is dim, but I do not mind. I am warm and safe, and the night is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been here for years, maybe since the first time I saw the light. The bark is rough and cold, and the floor is soft with leaves and moss. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have lived there for many years, and it is safe. The oak is strong, and the hollow is deep.
